newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore says race issue to persist in politics.
newsitem.headline: Singapore says race issue to persist in politics.

text.p: Singapore ruling People's Action Party (PAP), fresh from a sweeping election victory, said on Friday that divisive issues of race would continue to haunt the city-state's politics in the near term.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong used tough tactics to prevent what he called a Chinese chauvinist in the left-leaning Workers' Party from winning in a key constituency.
The PAP won there with 55 percent of the vote, well below its overall share of 65 percent.

Singapore, which is 77 percent ethnic Chinese with significant majorities of Malays and Tamils, will always have to contend with the potentially explosive issue of race in its politics, Goh Chok Tong said.

"The deep fault lines in our society over race, language, culture and religion will not go away. We must manage these emotional issues carefully," Goh told a news conference after the final results of Thursday's polls came in.

Goh said he had rolled out the PAP's big guns in Cheng San constituency to prevent Tang Liang Hong of the Workers' Party, whom he branded a Chinese chauvinist and anti-Christian, from gaining a seat in parliament.
"This is all nonsense," Tang had declared at a campaign rally. "I never said an Indian cannot become prime minister of Singapore. I never said a Malay cannot be prime minister of Singapore."
Goh said a failure of the PAP to fight Tang on the issue would be dangerous for Singapore's future and stability.

"Unless we take a clear stand now, there will be a powerful temptation for a Chinese electorate to push for a more prominent role for Chinese language and culture. This will be a very serious problem for Singapore," Goh said.

"Chinese Singaporeans, as the majority community, must always be mindful of the sensitivities of our minority communities. We are not a Chinese country and must never allow Chinese chauvinists to turn us into one," he added.
He said Singapore must never change its policy of using English as the common language to prevent one ethnic group from dominating the others.

Goh charged Tang with saying ethnic Chinese were "carrying the sedan chair" in Singapore instead of sitting in it. He said this was an attempt to divide a society that remembers race riots in the 1960s along "ethnic and linguistic lines".

"The fact that Tang could show up in Cheng San from nowhere and in nine days collect 45 percent of the vote shows how important it was for this issue to be put before the electorate and tackled during the campaign, even at the risk of losing some votes," Goh added.
